catalog_quote: Stress, i.e., which syllables are loudest and where the accent marks go in words, is a complex phenomenon in Kanza. As a general rule, stress tends to fall on either the first or second syllable in a word, with the second syllable being the most common, particularly in verbs. The addition of prefixes can move stress to the left, particularly verb pronoun prefixes without vowels, such as bl- in blúmiⁿ, 'I buy', from yumíⁿ, 'buy'. ... The stress of proper nouns, however, can be quite complicated indeed. ... [App. 22] Primary stress, or vowel loudness, is marked by way of an acute accent over the vowel receiving it, as in cedóⁿga, 'buffalo bull'. ... Longer words are generally stressed on either the first or second syllable, with secondary stress occurring regularly every other syllable thereafter. Secondary stress ... is often not written, except when it occurs in the word before the prim…

sources.quote: 'Accent in Proto-Siouan was normally on the second syllable of a word.' ... In Mississippi Valley Siouan 'Another major transformation is the loss of short, unaccented vowels in the initial syllable ... and the production of clusters that result from this syncopation' (citing Rankin et al. 2006 CSD). Comparative background only: explains why Dhegiha/Kansa words surface with first- OR second-syllable accent (bl-úmiⁿ < syncope of *wa-), consistent with the Reader's 'first or second syllable, prefixes move stress left'; no Kansa-specific rule stated.
sources.locator: sec. 'Proto-Siouan phonology' (tex line 73) and MVS section (tex line 237)
sources.note: Open comparative statement (Proto-Siouan 2nd-syllable accent; MVS initial-syllable syncope) that explains the Kansa 1st/2nd-syllable alternation historically; useful background note for the record, silent on synchronic Kansa rule.

sources.citation: Rankin, Robert L., Richard T. Carter & A. Wesley Jones. 1998. Proto-Siouan phonology and grammar. In Xingzhong Li, Luis Lopez & Tom Stroik (eds.), Papers from the 1997 Mid-America Linguistics Conference, 366-375. Columbia: University of Missouri-Columbia.
sources.note: Describes another variety (Glottolog siou1252). Reconstructs Proto-Siouan ACCENT as high vs. non-high pitch (possibly also a falling accent), 'probably pitch accent', iambic (second-syllable) placement with lengthening of the accented vowel; reports (after Rankin 1987) that in several Siouan languages, primarily Dhegiha, long vowels typically carry falling pitch which variably generates a syllable-final glottal stop, and argues glottalization may derive from a falling pitch accent.

tone.quote: Rankin (1987) shows that in several Siouan languages (primarily Dhegiha) long vowels typically have falling pitch. And this falling pitch automatically but variably generates a syllable-final glottal stop. If PSi had had phonemically independent falling pitch accent in addition to the high pitch that we now reconstruct, the glottalized stops and fricatives could have arisen as an allophonic feature of falling pitch. ... Languages with pitch accent systems tend to have a phonemic falling pitch in addition to simple high pitch. Yet we reconstruct PSi with only high pitch at the moment
tone.locator: inventory line 'ACCENT: high vs. non-high (possibly falling)'; 'Probably pitch accent'
tone.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone.summary: Proto-Siouan (and by implication Dhegiha incl. Kansa): pitch accent, H vs. non-H on the (historically second) accented syllable, accented vowels long, Dhegiha long vowels with falling pitch.

tone.quote: ´ primary accent; vowels marked with this symbol are louder and have a higher pitch than the rest of the word ` secondary accent; vowels marked with this symbol are louder and higher than unmarked vowels, but not as much as vowels with primary accent [p. xiv] ... ‘I go hunting’ is dáable. The first ‘a’ is pronounced a bit louder and is pitched a bit higher than the second ‘a’, approximately DAH-ah-bleh; the first two syllables run together with a falling tone. ... The rule of thumb: Every vowel in a Kaw is in a separate syllable. [pp. viii-ix]
tone.locator: Introduction, 'Symbols and abbreviations' p. xiv; 'A rule of thumb about pronunciation of vowels' pp. viii-ix
tone.summary: Word accent (primary/secondary) realized as loudness + high pitch, lexically placed on 1st or 2nd syllable and shifting with prefixes; falling pitch over VV sequences; no lexical tone claimed.
